findings.title: R2-RACE-1: a password change or a sign-in that was proved before a password reset is still applied after it. The in-flight change replaces the password the reset set, and the in-flight sign-in leaves a live session the reset never revoked
findings.root_cause: None of the credential writes checks, inside its own transaction, that the proof it rests on still holds, and the revocations bump no credential state that a later write could compare against. Sign-in (main.py:604-641) reads the verifier in find_login (accounts.py:192-200), runs 1 + PENDING_CHECKED scrypt derivations (main.py:611-622), and then create_session (accounts.py:212-232) inserts a live session. It never checks that identities.verifier is still the one it proved. Password change (auth_flows.py:505-519) reads the verifier (512), verifies it (513) and then calls new_verifier, which makes the Pwned Passwords range call (up to 2 s) and a scrypt (515). store.change (auth_flows.py:300-307) then calls _set_password (290-292): `UPDATE identities SET verifier=%s WHERE user_id=%s` has no `AND verifier = <proved>`, and the revocation keeps keep_token_hash without checking that this session is still live. FlowStore.reset (281-282), change (304-305) and revoke_all (accounts.py:238-242) take no lock that create_session or change would wait on. The 'sessions:<id>' advisory lock is taken only by create_session.
findings.evidence:
Committed failing tests (apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_race.py, commit cdf5d031) run concurrently in threads against the real Postgres cluster r2_race:
(1) test_a_password_change_in_flight_does_not_undo_a_password_reset holds the change at its Pwned check (the pwned_fetch test seam) while the owner runs forgot+reset in another browser. Result: the change answers 200 PASSWORD_CHANGED, then sign-in with the reset password gives 401 and with the change's password 200 ('assert (401, 200) == (200, 401)').
(2) test_a_sign_in_in_flight_does_not_outlive_a_password_reset holds the sign-in in its first derivation while the reset runs. Result: 'sign-in answered 200; live sessions 1; its session read answers 200'.
Probes without any hook (not committed): a holder of the old password looping sign-ins while the owner resets ended with a live session in 5 of 5 trials. A loop of password changes from a stolen session against one reset left the attacker's password as the account's in 3 of 5 runs. Four derivations take about 0.15 s here, and the change adds the Pwned API's network time. Contract: CONTRACT.md:114 (reset: 'every session revoked') and :154 ('Revoke all on password change or reset'). p3c-int 41067e7d changes none of auth_flows.py, accounts.py or main.py's sign-in (git diff ae9a1d8f 41067e7d is empty for them).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker holds the account's password and a session, for example from phishing. The owner notices and resets the password by email. (a) The attacker keeps password changes looping. Each one sets a password the attacker knows, and a successful change clears its own throttle (auth_flows.py:516). The change in flight when the reset commits overwrites the reset password. The owner's new password no longer works and the attacker signs in with his. (b) The attacker loops sign-ins with the old password. A successful sign-in clears the throttle (main.py:633), so the loop is unlimited. The sign-in in flight at the reset gets a session after the revocation and keeps it until the absolute lifetime ends, even though the reset revoked 'every session'. The same happens when the owner uses password change ('other sessions revoked') or sign-out-all followed by a change.
findings.general_class:
A security write authorised by a proof read earlier in the request (a verifier, a resolved session, an enrolment row) and applied without a compare-and-set on that proof in its own transaction, so a concurrent reset, change or revocation is not seen.
Sites today: switch-on sign-in (main.py:604-641); password change (auth_flows.py:505-519, 290-307); mfa/verify (auth_flows.py:544-591), which creates an MFA-passed session (584) and only then revokes the pending one (587), so a reset or sign-out-all between the request's resolve and line 584 leaves the new session live (same mechanism, not separately tested); and mfa/enroll (529-541), whose 'confirmed and not mfa_ok' check (532-534) is read in one transaction while the upsert (317-325) is unconditional.
Not affected: register/verify, which has no earlier session, and disable, because resolve checks u.status on every request (accounts.py:141).
Later tabs: Phase 4's admin 'revoke sessions' and role change (CONTRACT 4 'Revoke all ... disable, or role change'), the email change (email_codes purpose email_change), and Phase 5 checkout returns that set a plan from a state read before a cancellation all need the same compare-and-set.
3c: not in this class. The Terminal header is computed from each request's own principal.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c builds on the principal resolution and the plan catalog, not on the password, sign-in or MFA writes. The race lives only in the switch-on credential flows, which p3c-int leaves unchanged.
findings.affects_beta_live: The race is the same in both services, but the fix must cover every version that writes the shared tables. If beta carries the fixed sign-in/change and live an older one, live's in-flight sign-ins and changes still outlive a reset done on beta, and the reverse. A database-side guard helps here: the session insert and the verifier update conditioned on the identity's current verifier or a credential epoch, under one lock. So does shipping the fix to both services before either turns the switch on.
findings.fix:
Give the account a credential epoch, either users.credentials_changed_at or the identity row itself, locked by reset, change and revoke_all.
- create_session: run SELECT ... FROM identities WHERE user_id=%s FOR UPDATE in its own transaction and insert only if the verifier still equals the one the sign-in proved (else answer 401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS). Reset and change update that same row, so they serialise with it: a session made first is then seen and revoked by the reset's UPDATE sessions statement.
- Password change: `UPDATE identities SET verifier=new WHERE user_id=%s AND verifier=<proved>`, plus a check in the same transaction that the keep session is still live (FOR UPDATE, revoked_at IS NULL). Otherwise refuse with 401 or 409 and change nothing.
- mfa/verify: revoke the pending session first (`UPDATE ... WHERE token_hash=%s AND revoked_at IS NULL RETURNING`) and create the new session only if that returned a row, all in one transaction with the credential check.
- mfa/enroll: put the confirmed/mfa_ok condition into the upsert's WHERE.
The committed tests (test_r2_race.py: change vs reset, sign-in vs reset) must pass.
findings.related_r1: None. R1-7 (re-enrolment drops confirmed_at) and R1-9/R1-16 (throttles) are different mechanisms; R1-7's fix does not touch the sign-in or password-change writes.
findings.confirm_check: pytest apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_race.py -k 'in_flight' with EDGE_TEST_POSTGRES_URL set: both tests fail at ae9a1d8f with the messages quoted in the evidence.

findings.title: R2-RACE-4: a 'password changed' or 'account exists' email holds back the reset code that the email itself tells the owner to request at once. The forgot-password request answers 202 CODE_SENT and mails nothing for 60 s, and anyone holding a session can keep this up indefinitely
findings.root_cause: FlowStore._may_send (auth_flows.py:137-143) gates every code email: register, resend, forgot and restart. It refuses when ANY edge_bff.email_outbox row to the address is younger than RESEND_SECONDS, whatever the row's purpose: `SELECT 1 FROM email_outbox WHERE to_email=%s AND created_at > now() - 60 s`. Notification mails are rows of that same outbox: password_changed is enqueued by reset (286) and change (307), and account_exists by register (198). When the gate refuses, the route still answers the generic 202 ACCEPTED (auth_flows.py:483-488).
findings.evidence:
Committed failing tests (test_r2_race.py, commit cdf5d031):
- test_a_password_changed_email_does_not_hold_back_the_reset_it_asks_for: a password change, then forgot from another browser. Forgot answers {'status':'CODE_SENT','resend_after_s':60}, but no 'reset' row is queued ('assert 0 == 1').
- test_a_strangers_registration_does_not_hold_back_the_owners_reset: a stranger registers with the owner's address more than an hour after the account's own registration. The account_exists mail is queued, the owner's forgot then answers CODE_SENT, and no reset code is queued.
The password_changed text (email_texts.py:42-47) says 'If you did not, use "Forgot password?" on the sign-in page at once', and the account_exists text (34-39) also points to 'Forgot password?'.
I met this first while probing R2-RACE-1: a change loop running beside a reset made the owner's forgot silently send nothing (CODE_INVALID_OR_EXPIRED on the reset, because the latest code in the outbox was the old registration code).
findings.failure_scenario:
(a) Someone changes the owner's password from a stolen session. The owner gets the password_changed mail and follows it at once. Forgot answers 'code sent' and nothing arrives for a minute, so the owner may believe recovery is broken.
(b) The holder of a stolen session and the password changes the password at least once a minute. Each change needs only the current password, which the attacker set, and a success clears the change throttle. Every forgot of the owner then answers CODE_SENT and is never mailed. Each change also revokes the owner's sessions. The owner has no self-service way back; only the operator can help.
(c) A stranger who registers with the owner's address (once an hour, REGISTER_HOUR) holds the owner's reset back for 60 s, silently.
findings.general_class: One per-address send gate that counts every mail to the address, so mail made for another reason, or by another person, holds back the code that recovery needs, behind the same 202 CODE_SENT. All the notification mails reach it: password_changed from change and reset, and account_exists from a stranger's registration. Later senders reach it too: Phase 4 admin notices (role change, disable, an admin 'resend a code'), the Phase 4 email change (a code to the new address after a notice to the old one), and Phase 5 receipts, expiry reminders and payment-failure mails, each of which would hold the user's registration and reset codes back for 60 s.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c adds no mail and reads none of the auth flows.
findings.affects_beta_live: Both services would share one outbox and one 60-second gate, so a notification sent through either site holds back the codes of both. It is no worse otherwise.
findings.fix: Count only code mails in the 60-second gate: `AND purpose IN ('register','reset','email_change')` in _may_send, or a separate column marking the rows that carry a code. Keep notifications out of the per-address spacing; SEND_EMAIL's daily budget can still count them if wanted. Together with R2-RACE-1's fix, the owner can then recover against an attacker who holds a session. The two committed tests must pass.
findings.related_r1: R1-9 and R1-13 (limits keyed by a public identifier that others can drive: SEND_EMAIL, the one-live-code rule, the registration send budget). Their fixes concern those budgets and a proof-based way out, not the 60-second gate counting notification mail. The self-inflicted case (a) and the session-holder case (b) are not covered by them.
findings.confirm_check: pytest apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_race.py -k 'hold_back': both fail at ae9a1d8f with 'no reset code was queued'.

findings.title: R2-RACE-3: an MFA code confirms the enrolment that another session wrote after the code was checked. The admin is told 200 mfa_ok, the authenticator the admin scanned stops working, and the confirmed second factor is the other session's
findings.root_cause: mfa/verify (auth_flows.py:544-577) reads the enrolment row (store.totp, 553) and computes the matching step from that row's nonce (572-573). use_step (327-333) then confirms by user_id only: `UPDATE mfa_totp SET last_step=%s, confirmed_at=coalesce(confirmed_at, now()) ... WHERE user_id=%s AND (last_step IS NULL OR last_step < %s)`. Nothing ties the confirmation to the nonce that was checked. enroll (317-325) upserts a new nonce with confirmed_at NULL and last_step NULL. A pending (password-only) session may do so while the enrolment is unconfirmed (529-534).
findings.evidence: Committed failing test test_an_mfa_code_confirms_only_the_enrolment_it_was_checked_against (commit cdf5d031). The admin's verify is held after its code was checked (at use_step). Another pending session of the account then enrols (200) and the verify is released. It answers 200. Afterwards, on a fresh sign-in, the admin's authenticator answers 400 and the other session's answers 200: "the admin's authenticator now answers 400, the other session's answers 200". The test is outcome-based: it accepts a fix that refuses the verify or refuses the enrol.
findings.failure_scenario: At switch-on the admin (user #1) enrols for the first time (CONTRACT 4: 'enrols on first sign-in with the switch on'). An attacker with the admin password holds a pending session and repeatedly sends mfa/enroll, which has no throttle. If one enrol lands between the admin's code check and use_step, the admin sees MFA passed. The confirmed factor is the attacker's, and the attacker passes MFA with it from then on. The admin finds out only at the next sign-in. The window is milliseconds, and a pending session can already replace an unconfirmed enrolment by design, so the exploit is narrow. The mechanism, though, is exactly what R1-7's fix will rely on.
findings.general_class: A confirmation or consumption written by key only after a check against a value read earlier, so what is confirmed is the row as it is now, not the row that was checked. Sites: use_step (auth_flows.py:327-333). Safe today: email codes, consumed by the code_id read FOR UPDATE (169-176, 236, 279), and recovery codes, matched by code_hash (335-342). Later: R1-7's fix (a pending re-enrolment kept beside the confirmed one) must confirm the nonce it checked. So must the Phase 4 email change (confirm the target_email of the code checked) and the Phase 5 payment confirmation (confirm the checkout, amount and plan that were checked, not the account's current pending one).
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c does not touch MFA.
findings.affects_beta_live: The same in both services. The fix belongs in the UPDATE's WHERE clause, so it holds whichever version runs.
findings.fix: Bind the nonce: `use_step(user_id, step, nonce)` with `AND nonce = %s`, answering MFA_CODE_INVALID when no row matches. Better, run the whole verify under the mfa_totp row lock: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, check, confirm or count, commit in one transaction. That also fixes R2-RACE-2. The enroll upsert should carry its permission condition in its WHERE (R2-RACE-1 site).
findings.related_r1: R1-7 (an MFA-passed re-enrolment drops confirmed_at). Its proposed fix, keeping the confirmed enrolment until the new one is proved, is defeated if the pending replacement can be swapped between the check and the confirmation. use_step must bind the nonce it checked.
findings.confirm_check: pytest apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_race.py -k mfa_code_confirms: fails at ae9a1d8f.

findings.title: R2-RACE-2: MFA tries sent together all pass the consecutive-failure check. A burst at 99 TOTP failures reaches 104, and a burst after a recovery lock ended has 5 codes checked where 2 are allowed
findings.root_cause: mfa/verify decides the NIST cap and the lock from a row read in its own transaction (store.totp, auth_flows.py:553, decided at 563-570). lock_over (352-357) restarts the count in a second transaction and mfa_failed (344-350) adds the failure in a third. No lock of the account is held across the read, the code check and the count. The only atomic limit is MFA_USER (10 per 15 min, Throttle.attempt), so up to 10 tries per window pass a read that sees the same count.
findings.evidence:
Committed failing test test_a_burst_at_the_mfa_cap_checks_only_the_tries_left, two cases (commit cdf5d031). Five tries are released together after each has read the row.
- TOTP at 99 consecutive failures: '5 of 5 parallel code tries were checked (allowed 1) ... consecutive failures now 104'.
- Recovery lock ended a second ago (count 10): '5 of 5 parallel recovery_code tries were checked (allowed 2) ... consecutive failures now 13'.
A probe without any barrier (10 tries released by one Event, 5 trials) ended at 104, 105, 104, 105 and 106 consecutive TOTP failures from 99. The code comment at auth_flows.py:556-557 states 'at most 100 consecutive failed codes per account (NIST SP 800-63B-4)'.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with the admin password (a pending session) sends 10 TOTP guesses at once each time the count is below the cap or a lock has just ended. Each crossing of the cap gives up to 9 extra checked guesses beyond the 100, and each lock end gives the full MFA_USER window instead of the restart allowance (TOTP 10, recovery 2). That allowance was the N2 decision. With 6-digit TOTP the gain per cycle is small, so the severity is non-blocking. The guarantee the code documents, though, does not hold under concurrency.
findings.general_class:
A failure counter decided by a read in one transaction and counted in another, with nothing locking the account in between: concurrent tries all pass the read. Sites: mfa_totp totp_failures and recovery_failures, and lock_over (auth_flows.py:344-357, 553-579).
Checked safe: SIGNIN_LOGIN, MFA_USER and change:<id>, decided and counted under one advisory lock (throttle.py:68-81; probe: 25 parallel wrong sign-ins gave 10 checked and 15 answered 429). The email-code attempts (FOR UPDATE) and CODE_USER (under the email advisory lock; probe: 25 parallel wrong reset codes counted 20) are also safe.
Later: R1-16's per-account password cap, if built like the MFA one; Phase 4 admin lock and unlock; and Phase 5 once-only or limited-use rules (trial once, promo-code uses, payment retries) must decide and count under one lock.
3c's terminal-api quotas use lock_subscriber (p3c-int store.py) and are not in this class.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c's quotas decide and count under terminal-api's per-subscriber advisory lock (p3c-int apps/terminal-api/app/store.py lock_subscriber), and MFA is not on the 3c path.
findings.affects_beta_live: No change: the race goes through the shared database, whatever the number of services.
findings.fix: Do the verify's decision, the code check, the confirmation or count, and the lock in one transaction under the mfa_totp row lock: `SELECT ... FROM mfa_totp WHERE user_id=%s FOR UPDATE`, then lock_over, use_step or use_recovery, and mfa_failed on the same connection. The code check is a few HMACs, so holding the row lock is cheap. This is the same change that closes R2-RACE-3. The parametrised committed test must pass.
findings.related_r1: R1-16 (no per-account password cap). The MFA cap it cites as the model is the one this race breaks.
findings.confirm_check: pytest apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_race.py -k burst_at_the_mfa_cap: both cases fail at ae9a1d8f.

findings.title: R2-RACE-5: two edge-bff services on one database with different EDGE_MULTIUSER values fight over the shared rows. The switch-off service's worker and backtest loop claim switch-on accounts' queued jobs and end them FAILED CAPABILITY_REQUIRED, and its start-up puts the environment password back on user #1
findings.root_cause: Every edge-bff runs the background loops by default (config.py:48, 109: EDGE_WORKER_ENABLED defaults to true). They claim from tables shared by all services: edge_bff.jobs (store.py claim, SKIP LOCKED) and edge_bff.backtest_jobs (backtest.py:650-660). Each loop then decides the job by the claiming service's own configuration: Worker.refused (worker.py:79-94) and BacktestLoop.dispatch (backtest.py:937-944) use owner_principal (principal.py:347-351). With the switch off, that maps any owner except EDGE_ADMIN_OWNERS to a principal with no capability. At start, AccountStore.seed (accounts.py:121-124), run from main.py's lifespan, copies EDGE_PASSWORD_VERIFIER onto user #1's identity whenever the starting service's switch is off.
findings.evidence: Probe, run on the r2_race cluster and not committed because the beta/live design is not decided. App A (switch on) and app B (switch off) share one Store. A paid chat user submits a run on A. B's worker claims and executes it: 'JOBS [{... state: FAILED, error_code: CAPABILITY_REQUIRED}] live orc asked []', so the job never reached Orc. A second probe: user #1's verifier is changed, as a password change on A would do, then B is started. Afterwards the changed password no longer verifies and EDGE_PASSWORD_VERIFIER's does ('SEED False True'). The backtest loop takes the same path by reading (backtest.py:764-765 and 937-944).
findings.failure_scenario: The user's plan (EXEC.md 'Production environment', 2026-11-19) has the beta at the Railway address, where 'every feature is tried', and the live site at the user's domain, sharing one database. If beta turns EDGE_MULTIUSER on while live is still off, a share of the beta users' AI runs and backtests (those live's loops claim first) ends FAILED CAPABILITY_REQUIRED with no Orc call. And if the admin changes or resets a password on beta because it leaked, every live restart or deploy restores the environment's (leaked) password for user #1 on the shared database. Today, with one service, the same happens only during a deploy that flips the switch, while the old and new deployments overlap.
findings.general_class:
A background loop that claims from tables shared by every edge-bff service and decides each claimed row by the claiming service's own configuration and code; and a start-up step that writes shared rows by the starting service's configuration. Sites: the AI worker (worker.py), the backtest loop (backtest.py) and the seed (accounts.py:121-124). The email sender runs only with the switch on and is fenced by its lease, so it is safe. cleanup_sessions and purge_pending are harmless when run twice.
Later: 3c adds no loop. Phase 4 admin jobs and Phase 5's payment reconciliation and subscription-expiry loops would run in both services unless fenced. Any change of a dispatch check (3e page locks, new capability names) would be applied to the other site's jobs by whichever version claims them.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c adds no background loop, and its per-owner terminal-api rows are keyed by owner. The finding is about which edge-bff service's loop and start-up touch the shared edge_bff tables.
findings.affects_beta_live: This finding appears only with two edge-bff services on one database. It blocks running beta and live with different EDGE_MULTIUSER values or different dispatch code. Options: run the loops in one service only (EDGE_WORKER_ENABLED=false on the other) and only in a switch-on service, or give jobs a site/version column the claim filters on. In either case, stop the switch-off seed from overwriting user #1's identity while the shared database holds switch-on accounts.
findings.fix: Not a code defect of the single-service deploy. It is a constraint the beta/live design must take into the open questions (EXEC.md 'Production environment'). Either both services share the switch state and one version of the dispatch checks, with EDGE_WORKER_ENABLED on only one of them, or jobs carry the site that made them and each loop claims only its own. Also make AccountStore.seed skip the verifier copy when the database already holds switch-on accounts (any 'u_' owner, or a password change recorded on the identity). Record the decision with the beta/live plan.
findings.related_r1: R1-5 and R1-31 (process caches in front of per-owner calls) are a different mechanism: per-process memory, not shared-table claims.
findings.confirm_check: Two create_app instances on one store, one with multiuser=True and one with the switch off. Submit a run as a switch-on paid user on the first, then run store.claim and the second app's worker.execute: the job ends FAILED CAPABILITY_REQUIRED. Start the second app after changing user #1's verifier: the verifier is reset to settings.password_verifier.

checked: Setup: branch r2-race at ae9a1d8f; Postgres cluster r2_race on port 55532, stopped at the end; one commit, cdf5d031, holding only apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_race.py (7 failing tests); worktree clean afterwards.
Read r1_seen.json (46 findings plus refuter notes) and did not re-report R1-7, R1-9, R1-10, R1-13, R1-16 or R1-28; where my findings touch them, related_r1 says why their fixes miss it.
Throttle.attempt (throttle.py:68-81): the decision and the count share one advisory xact lock. Probe: 25 parallel wrong sign-ins gave 10 checked (401) and 15 refused (429). Not exploitable.

Email code tries are serialised by FlowStore._lock (email advisory lock) plus the code row FOR UPDATE. Probe: 25 parallel wrong reset codes gave 20 CODE_USER counts and at most 5 attempts per code. Not exploitable.
Username race: two pending registrations of different addresses verifying the same username at once answered 200 and 409 USERNAME_TAKEN (savepoint plus users_username_key). Safe.

Session cap: 12 parallel correct sign-ins left 5 live sessions (create_session under the 'sessions:<id>' lock). Two of the 12 got 429 because SIGNIN_LOGIN counts tries rather than failures; that belongs to the R1-9 class and is not new.

TOTP replay is atomic (use_step 'last_step < step'); recovery codes are single-use by an atomic UPDATE; concurrent enrol upserts serialise on the mfa_totp primary key, and the recovery-code DELETE/INSERT stays consistent.

AI jobs: submit under the 'jobs:'+owner lock with UNIQUE(owner_key, submission_key) and one active job per owner; claim uses SKIP LOCKED with a lease; heartbeat, attempted and transition are fenced by lease_token; stop_queued and claim are ordered by the row lock; refused() runs before attempted and again on redispatch.

Backtest jobs: submit under the 'backtest:'+owner lock, with the QUEUED count and the cap read under that lock and a UNIQUE key; client_request_id replays return the same job; claim uses SKIP LOCKED plus the backtest_jobs_one_running_owner unique index; the worker's 409 BUSY is handled; _FENCE guards every follower write; dispatch re-reads the principal on every iteration.

Email outbox: claim with SKIP LOCKED and a 60 s lease against a 15 s send timeout; sent and failed fenced by lease_token; Resend Idempotency-Key per row; webhook svix-id applied once with ON CONFLICT.

Per-owner stores are locked: preferences PUT (advisory lock, FOR UPDATE version check, key and byte limits under the lock), and the saved-item caps of layouts, presets, drawings, watchlist and screener items, the star sharing the 'watchlist:' lock with the watchlist.

purge_pending vs verify_registration: the FOR UPDATE row lock and re-evaluation of the WHERE clause keep a just-verified account; restart vs purge is guarded by WHERE status='pending'. seed and seed_subscription are safe across replicas (advisory locks).
Client side, two tabs with different accounts: edge-session.ts send() refuses a write whose identity changed (USER_CHANGED) and repeats a CSRF_INVALID write only for the same identity.
SSE: still_signed_in re-resolves on each loop (R1-28 covers its missing test). X-Edge-Entitlements comes from the request's single resolved principal (FastAPI dependency cache).

p3c-int 41067e7d: auth_flows.py, accounts.py, mfa.py, mailer.py, worker.py, principal.py, store.py and main.py's sign-in are unchanged from ae9a1d8f, so R2-RACE-1 to 4 are present there too. terminal-api owner rows are made with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; quotas are checked under lock_subscriber; edge-bff's terminal_http client is created lazily without an await (no race).

Natural probes without hooks, not committed: a sign-in loop vs a reset left a live session in 5 of 5 trials; a change loop vs a reset left the attacker's password in 3 of 5 runs; 10 parallel TOTP tries at 99 reached 104-106 consecutive failures in 5 of 5 trials.
Beta/live probe, not committed: a switch-off app's worker ended a switch-on user's run FAILED CAPABILITY_REQUIRED, and its start-up restored EDGE_PASSWORD_VERIFIER onto user #1's identity.

Two-instance overlap during a Railway deploy (Dockerfile runs one uvicorn worker; railway.ts has 1 replica): the only shared-state effect found is R2-RACE-5. A brief deadlock between two outbox claims is possible and heals itself (logged and retried), so it is not reported.

findings.title: A switch-on session that has not passed MFA (or is idle, or belongs to a disabled user #1) becomes a full '*' admin session under any edge-bff running with EDGE_MULTIUSER off
findings.root_cause: The switch-off resolution (principal.py:298-302) reads the session with store.session (store.py:88-90), which checks only token_hash, revoked_at and expires_at, then accepts it when owner_key == EDGE_OWNER and returns switch_off_principal with mfa_ok=True and '*' (principal.py:184-194). A switch-on sign-in of user #1 writes a session row with that same owner_key (accounts.py create_session inserts user['owner_key'], which is EDGE_OWNER for the seed row) and mfa_passed_at NULL while MFA is pending. The switch-off path never looks at user_id, mfa_passed_at, last_seen_at or users.status, although the column comment of migration 20261116_003:136 says a switch-off session is the one with user_id NULL. Every pre-Phase-1 build does the same check (637b0b96 main.py:314-320, store.py:68-70, the build of rollback target 150686f9).
findings.evidence: Failing test apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_skew.py::test_a_switch_on_session_that_has_not_passed_mfa_opens_nothing_with_the_switch_off. A switch-on app signs in user #1 with the password only and gets 403 MFA_REQUIRED, and /api/v1/conversations answers MFA_REQUIRED. The row is user_id set, mfa_passed_at NULL, owner_key = EDGE_OWNER. The same cookie on a switch-off app on the same database gets 200 /api/v1/auth/session with access {role: admin, mfa_ok: true, capabilities: ['*'], version: 'env'}. A control sign-in made with the switch off still works. p3c-int does not touch store.py or principal.py (git diff --stat bf273f52 41067e7d is empty for them).
findings.failure_scenario: Switch on (Phase 6). An attacker who knows only the admin's password signs in and keeps the pending-MFA cookie (valid 24 h, EDGE_SESSION_SECONDS). Then one of three things happens: the switch goes back to false, which is the documented way back; edge-bff is rolled back to any build before Phase 1; or the Railway deployment overlap of the switch-on deploy is still running the old switch-off container. In each case that cookie is a full admin session: every tab, the manual Orc agent (admin.manual) and owner edge-private's conversations, with no TOTP. Idle sessions past EDGE_SESSION_IDLE_SECONDS and a disabled user #1 are accepted the same way.
findings.general_class: One table read by two resolvers of different strength (switch-off and switch-on, or old and new build), where the weaker one accepts rows the stronger one wrote under stricter rules. Other sites: any later session state, such as step-up, 'next: verify/pay' for Phase 5 or a session per site. The email codes and MFA rows that a switch-off build ignores do not open anything, because switch-off never reads them. The rollback runbook of Phase 6 has the same hole: pre-Phase-1 builds cannot be fixed, so their rollback must revoke switch-on sessions first.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c reads the principal that this resolution returns but does not change how a session is resolved.
findings.affects_beta_live: Worse. With a beta edge-bff on the switch off and a live one on the switch on, sharing edge_bff.sessions, every pending live admin session is a full admin session on the beta host. The cookie is host-only, so the attacker copies their own cookie, which is exactly the MFA threat model. Sessions are not bound to the site that made them: no column, and resolve does not check one. So a 'who may sign in to the beta' rule enforced only at sign-in is bypassed by moving a live cookie, and with a shared EDGE_SESSION_SECRET the CSRF token works across sites too. A switch-off beta is in any case an MFA-free door to user #1 on the shared database.
findings.fix: The switch-off resolver accepts only rows made by the switch-off sign-in: add 'AND user_id IS NULL' to store.session, or in principal.resolve refuse a row with user_id set. The switch-on rollback runbook (Phase 6, records) revokes every session with user_id IS NOT NULL before any switch-off or pre-Phase-1 build starts. If the beta/live plan keeps a switch-off site, record that this site must not share the database, or add a site column to sessions.

findings.title: Every edge-bff start with the switch off copies EDGE_PASSWORD_VERIFIER over user #1's password identity, undoing a password change made with the switch on (the old password signs in again)
findings.root_cause: AccountStore.seed runs at every start (main.py lifespan, auth.seed_user, principal.py seed_user). For an existing user #1 with multiuser False it runs UPDATE identities SET verifier = EDGE_PASSWORD_VERIFIER (accounts.py:121-124). Nothing tells the seed's own copy apart from a verifier the account set through /api/v1/auth/password/change or a reset (auth_flows.py:290-292, 504-519). README.md:795 promises the opposite for switch on: 'the identity is the account's own and is never overwritten'.
findings.evidence: Failing test apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_skew.py::test_a_switch_off_start_keeps_the_password_user_one_changed_with_the_switch_on. On a switch-on app, user #1 passes MFA and changes its password (200). One switch-off start on the same database follows. The identity's verifier is then the env one again. Signing in with the switch on, the replaced old password is accepted (403 MFA_REQUIRED) and the new one is refused (401).
findings.failure_scenario: The admin rotates their password on the switch-on site, for example after the env password leaked. A later switch-off start silently restores the old password as valid for the switch-on sign-in: the switch's way back, a rollback, or any restart while the switch is off. The admin's own new password stops working when the switch is on again.
findings.general_class: A start-up step that rewrites a row from configuration whenever the process's mode is X, while another mode, version or process lets the user change that row. The same shape would reach any later setting the seed copies from env, such as the email of user #1 or its role, and any Phase 4 admin edit of a seeded row.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c does not touch the seed or the identities table.
findings.affects_beta_live: Worse and constant. With a switch-off beta and a switch-on live on one database, every beta deploy resets the live admin's password to EDGE_PASSWORD_VERIFIER, and every push to main that touches apps/edge-bff deploys the beta. The constraint must be recorded: either both sites run the same switch value, or the seed never copies while any switch-on site uses the database.
findings.fix: Copy the env verifier only while the identity still holds the seed's own copy. For example, keep a marker column (source = 'env') that password change and reset clear, or compare against the last verifier the seed wrote. Then document the rule in the README switch table, and keep the switch-off sign-in reading EDGE_PASSWORD_VERIFIER directly as it does today (main.py sign_in).

findings.title: The start-up readiness is read once, but /ready is read on every healthcheck: a start during a database outage or before its migration serves traffic with no AI job worker, clean-up or email sender, and a never-ready build still runs the backtest job loop
findings.root_cause: lifespan (main.py:240-278) calls store.ready once. On failure, ready['value'] stays False for the process: no seed of user #1 or its plan, no capability names, no AI worker loop (:272) and so no hourly cleanup_sessions (worker.py run, store.py:354), and no email sender (:277-278). The /ready route (main.py:399-405) reads store.ready again on every call, so once the database or the migration is there, Railway's healthcheck (/ready, timeout 120 s, railway.ts:251) passes and marks the deployment SUCCESS. The backtest loop (:275) starts whatever readiness says ('it does not wait for /ready'). With the switch on, its dispatch reads accounts.owner, and the UndefinedTable from a missing catalog is not caught: dispatch catches only psycopg.OperationalError (backtest.py:935). The claimed job is therefore left RUNNING until reap ends it FAILED WORKER_LOST (backtest.py:639-648).
findings.evidence: Two failing tests in apps/edge-bff/tests/test_r2_skew.py. (1) test_a_start_during_a_database_outage_runs_the_ai_worker_once_it_is_ready: the first readiness read fails, /ready then answers 200, a run is accepted 202 and stays QUEUED. A control probe with no outage reaches FINISHED. (2) test_a_build_that_is_not_ready_claims_no_backtest_job: a build whose /ready answers 503 claims a backtest queued by the serving build, posts it to the worker and stores it FINISHED. The deploy steps rely on the opposite: EXEC.md:15535 and :15638 say 'a build deployed before the migration never takes traffic'. The latch predates Phase 0 (83ca29d4 main.py:215-224), but Phases 0-2 put the seed, the plan seed, the names and the email sender behind it.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) edge-bff starts while Postgres restarts (about 12 s, the twice-daily postgres-memory-cron or a manual restart) or while the database is briefly unreachable. The deployment goes SUCCESS, the old one is removed, every Monitor question stays 'queued' forever, sessions, throttle rows and pending registrations are never purged, and with the switch on no registration or reset code is ever mailed, until someone restarts edge-bff. (b) A build pushed before its migration, with the migration applied within the 120 s window, is the same. (c) A build that never becomes ready is killed after 120 s. Meanwhile its backtest loop claims queued jobs and dispatches them with its new code, and with the switch on turns each into WORKER_LOST.
findings.general_class: A readiness decision taken once at start for background loops, while the readiness probe is recomputed and gates traffic. The two disagree in both directions. Any later loop started in lifespan inherits it: the Phase 4 admin jobs, the Phase 5 payment reconciliation and the 3e example refresh.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c adds no start-up step or loop (its lifespan is unchanged on p3c-int), and its migrations come first in its order.
findings.affects_beta_live: Worse: two services multiply the starts, and a silent no-worker instance on one site leaves its jobs to the other site's loop, if that loop runs at all.
findings.fix: Run the start-up steps and start the AI worker, email sender and backtest loop from one background task that retries readiness every poll until it succeeds. Do not start any loop before that. Log 'startup_not_ready' while waiting. Optionally make /ready answer 503 until the start-up steps have run.

findings.title: 3c's entitlement header has no acknowledgement: a terminal-api below 3c (rollback or upload mix-up) silently ignores x-terminal-capabilities and serves a capped principal in full (locked datasets of a partly allowed /bundle, every yearly file, no per-owner quota)
findings.root_cause: The deployed terminal-api reads no x-terminal-capabilities at all, and says it ignores the gateway's owner header 'until T2' (ae9a1d8f apps/terminal-api/app/main.py:45-47). A gateway key is always Caller('gateway', email=proxy_subscriber) (:276-277). On p3c-int, edge-bff sends the headers and relays whatever comes back (main.py:555-588) without checking that terminal-api applied them; no response field or header carries the applied version. Its refuse-first check stops only a request whose tickers or every dataset are locked. A /bundle with at least one allowed dataset is forwarded with the locked ones left for terminal-api to mark (terminal_access.py:219-220), and the history window is enforced only by terminal-api.
findings.evidence: Code read in both versions. The deployed terminal-api's identify has no capability path, and grep finds no CAPS header in apps/terminal-api/app at ae9a1d8f. p3c-int forward_terminal and relay_cut read only status, content type, JSON and cut headers. CONTRACT 8b (p3c-int) gives deploy steps 1-5 forward only, with no terminal-api rollback floor. terminal-api deploys by hand (CLI upload, not gated, RAILWAY_CHANGELOG Phase 0 step 6), so an older archive or a Railway redeploy of an older deployment (e.g. 80bec768) is a normal operation.
findings.failure_scenario: Switch on, a free principal (terminal.dataset {ids:[price]}, history_days 730, tickers [BBCA]). terminal-api is rolled back below 3c, or a 3c edge-bff runs before step 2. The page's /bundle {ticker: BBCA, datasets: [price, broker]} passes edge-bff's check (one dataset allowed) and the old terminal-api presigns broker flow files and every yearly price file. The free user gets broker data and the full history, and usage goes to the gateway row with its 1e9 override, so D6's per-owner quotas vanish. With the switch off the owner is admin, so nothing shows.
findings.general_class: An entitlement sent to another, separately deployed service with no proof that the receiver understood it: the older receiver ignores an unknown header and fails open. The workers' context is the safe contrast: a pre-3b worker refuses the unknown context.allow and fails closed. The same risk applies to Orc when the AI opens to plans (the X-Saniti-Capabilities header of CONTRACT 7, R1-6) and to any Phase 4/5 entitlement passed to a worker or terminal-api.
findings.affects_3c_why: The fix belongs in 3c's own wire (terminal-api and edge-bff on p3c-int) before deploy step 3, while both sides are still being built.
findings.affects_beta_live: Worse: the shared terminal-api follows beta. If it is ever rolled back for beta, both sites' capped users are served in full.
findings.fix: terminal-api echoes the applied entitlement on every answer to an owner call, for example a response header x-terminal-capabilities-applied: 1 <version>. edge-bff (forward_terminal, relay_cut, PageFiles) answers 503 TERMINAL_UNAVAILABLE for a non-admin principal when the echo is missing or differs. Add a test with a fake pre-3c terminal-api. Record a rollback floor: while EDGE_MULTIUSER is on, terminal-api is never rolled back below 3c.

findings.title: 3c header: one dataset id that the receiving terminal-api does not know fails every Terminal call of the account with 400; with the paid plan's terminal.dataset {all:true} a dataset added to edge-bff before terminal-api breaks every paid user
findings.root_cause: parse_capabilities refuses a datasets entry that is not in this terminal-api's DATASETS (p3c-int entitlements.py:131), an unknown quota name (:145), an extra field (:109) and any v other than 1 (:113). owner_of turns that into 400 invalid_owner_headers for the whole request (main.py:322). edge-bff builds 'datasets' from its own compiled DATASET_IDS (terminal_access.py:51-55, :97), so the paid plan's '{"all": true}' (20261117_003:227) sends every id this edge-bff build knows. tests/test_terminal_access.py compares the two lists only inside one commit. The two services deploy separately: edge-bff automatically on a green push, terminal-api by a hand upload.
findings.evidence: Probe on p3c-int's entitlements.py (extracted to the scratchpad and run with python -I). The same lists parse. When edge-bff is one dataset ahead ('fx'), the result is HeaderError on field datasets: "'fx' is not a dataset of this terminal-api". When terminal-api is one dataset behind (no 'yield'), the result is HeaderError: "'yield' is not a dataset of this terminal-api".
findings.failure_scenario: Switch on. A commit adds a dataset to both services. The push deploys edge-bff after CI, and terminal-api is uploaded later, which is the natural order for a GitHub-connected edge-bff and a CLI-uploaded terminal-api. Until the upload, every Terminal, Backtest-preview and Watchlist-logo call of every paid user answers 400 (relayed as is, R1-1). A dataset removed or renamed on terminal-api does the same to every older edge-bff.
findings.general_class: An allow-list on a wire whose vocabulary is compiled into two separately deployed services, where an unknown id fails the whole request instead of being 'not granted'. R1-22's fix (a declared value domain per capability in the catalog) does not cover this, because the catalog value {all:true} is valid and the expansion happens in code. The workers are the tolerant contrast (allowOf accepts unknown ids). Later sites: the 3e lock lists, the Phase 4 per-plan quota names and the Orc capabilities when the AI opens.
findings.affects_3c_why: It is 3c's own parse and header builder; the cheap fix is to change them before deploy.
findings.affects_beta_live: Worse: the shared terminal-api follows beta, so any dataset or quota name beta drops breaks every capped user of an older live edge-bff, and a v2 terminal-api must keep accepting v1.
findings.fix: In parse_capabilities, drop and log an unknown dataset id (it is not served anyway, so this fails closed). Keep the refusal for unknown restriction fields and quota names, or announce terminal-api's dataset list (in /state or the manifest) and have edge-bff send only ids terminal-api has announced. Record the order rule: add on terminal-api first, remove on edge-bff first.

findings.title: Recorded rollback points are listed per service with no order or compatibility floor: a worker rolled back alone refuses every call of the deployed edge-bff; after 3c's planned steps, the pre-3b and pre-3c edge-bff rollback targets fail every call
findings.root_cause: The Phase 3b record lists 'Rollback points: backtest-worker b087e1c4, screener-worker 0b517ec0, edge-bff 49e7cf88' (RAILWAY_CHANGELOG.md:15) and each step says only 'Rollback: the deployment live before' (EXEC.md:15890, :15897). The pre-3b workers refuse every context key but their known ones. At 848a9d41, backtest-worker server.ts:75 (UNKNOWN_FIELD context.<k>) and :239 (job context: only job_id, prior_trials, owner_trials, rights) refuse it, and so does screener-worker run.ts:69 (closed(c, ['rights'])). The deployed edge-bff 335d78b3 sends allow and limits on every call. On p3c-int, step 3 makes allow required (access.ts:45-46, run.ts:101 and :114), so edge-bff 49e7cf88 and older fail every worker call. 3c step 4 (terminal-api requires the owner headers) makes every pre-3c edge-bff fail every Terminal call. The p3c-int CONTRACT 8b gives no rollback floor for either.
findings.evidence: Code at 848a9d41 (pre-3b workers), ae9a1d8f (the 3b edge-bff's context_of in allow.py), and p3c-int 41067e7d (required allow). The records cited above. git show 41067e7d CONTRACT.md has no rollback guidance for 3c beyond the migration comment of 20261118_001.
findings.failure_scenario: A Backtest bug after 3b is rolled back by redeploying backtest-worker b087e1c4 alone. Every validate, signals and job call of the live edge-bff 335d78b3 is then refused UNKNOWN_FIELD context.allow, and queued jobs end FAILED at dispatch. The same happens to the Screener with 0b517ec0. After the 3b follow-up, a rollback of edge-bff to its last recorded target 49e7cf88 fails every Backtest and Screener call with INVALID_CONTEXT. After 3c step 4, a rollback to 335d78b3 breaks the Terminal, the page files and the Backtest preview.
findings.general_class: Expand-and-contract deploy steps across separately deployed services, where each step moves the floor of the other side's safe rollback target and nothing records it. The same applies to 3c steps 1-5, the 3b follow-up migration (which deletes the backtest/screener families the 3b edge-bff reads), 3d (publisher vs edge-bff), the worker limits keys when plans set them (CONTRACT 15: workers first), and the release-stage vocabulary (the trigger in 20261117_003:122-127 and releases.STAGES: a new stage must reach code before any row uses it).
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c's deploy order (with the 3b follow-up's step 3) is what moves the floors, so its runbook should state them before it runs.
findings.affects_beta_live: Worse: the shared workers and terminal-api follow beta, and the strict wires (worker context, the v1 header) accept only the shapes of their version. Every contract step on beta sets a floor for the live edge-bff version, and a 'push ke live' of an older tested build can land below it.
findings.fix: For 3b, the 3b follow-up and 3c, record a compatibility table: for each step, which rollback target of each service stays valid. Worker rollback needs edge-bff rolled back first. After step 3 the edge-bff floor is 335d78b3. After 3c step 4 it is the 3c build, and terminal-api's floor is 3c while the switch is on. Add the beta/live rule that the live edge-bff stays at or above the floors the shared services impose.

findings.title: Beta/live on one database: each edge-bff's background loops claim the other site's rows (AI jobs, backtest jobs, email outbox) and process them under their own switch, settings and code
findings.root_cause: The queues have no site or version column, and every claim takes any row (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED): edge_bff.jobs (store.py:185-197), backtest_jobs (backtest.py:650-666) and email_outbox (mailer.py:73-91). The claiming instance then decides with its own settings. Backtest dispatch re-reads the owner's principal through its own owner_principal (backtest.py:933-945), which with the switch off is switch_off_principal (no capability for a u_ owner). The AI worker's re-check works the same way (worker.py refused). The email sender delivers by its own EDGE_EMAIL_MODE, and log mode marks the row sent while keeping the payload (mailer.py:178-185).
findings.evidence: Probe /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-saniti/f3bec3b8-f6e3-5a54-b257-4a56b384bdc8/scratchpad/r2skew/probe_beta_live_backtest_loop.py (run on cluster r2_skew, not committed). A paid account on a switch-on app submits a backtest. A switch-off app with the loop on shares the database, claims the job and ends it FAILED {code: CAPABILITY_REQUIRED, capability: backtest.run, message: 'This feature is not part of your EDGE plan...'}. The worker never got the job. The mailer evidence is from the code: the claim has no filter, and delivery reads self.settings.email_mode.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) A live paid user's backtest is taken by the beta's loop (switch off) and refused as 'not part of your plan'. (b) A beta in EDGE_EMAIL_MODE=log takes live registration and reset emails. The user never gets the code, and the code stays readable in email_outbox.payload, which validate() forbids outside dev for the switch-on site itself. (c) A beta deploy, which happens on every main push touching apps/edge-bff, kills the live users' backtests that beta's loop holds: they end WORKER_LOST, never resubmitted. M340's 'no active run' check before each deploy would have to count both sites. (d) The hourly purge of the older version applies its rules (pending users after 24 h, throttle after 2 days) to rows written by the newer version.
findings.general_class: Shared work queues and housekeeping consumed by heterogeneous consumers (different config or version) with no routing key. The same will reach the Phase 5 payment reconciliation and webhooks, the Phase 4 admin jobs, and any per-site setting a loop reads (the Orc or worker URLs, releases.json, EDGE_ADMIN_OWNERS).
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c adds no queue or loop; only the beta/live plan creates the second consumer.
findings.affects_beta_live: This finding exists only with two edge-bff services on one database (the user's 2026-11-19 plan). With one service, the Railway deploy overlap gives the same effect for seconds only, between builds of the same configuration.
findings.fix: For the beta/live design (open details): either one site runs the loops (EDGE_WORKER_ENABLED=false on the other, recorded), or every queued row carries the site that made it and each claim filters on it. The email sender must run where the switch-on mode is resend. Extend M340 to both sites.

findings.title: Beta/live on one database: three per-service secrets key shared rows (EDGE_SESSION_SECRET for auth_throttle and CSRF, EDGE_CODE_SECRET for email_codes, EDGE_MFA_KEY for the one mfa_totp row per user), and nothing records that both services must hold the same values
findings.root_cause: Throttle key hashes are HMAC with EDGE_SESSION_SECRET (throttle.py:64, main.py:226), and so are sessions.created_ip_hash and the CSRF token (security.py:46-47). email_codes.code_hash is HMAC with EDGE_CODE_SECRET (auth_flows.py:126-128). The TOTP secret and the recovery-code hashes derive from EDGE_MFA_KEY (mfa.py:24, :61), and mfa_totp holds one row per user, replaced on enrolment (auth_flows.py:317-320). CONTRACT 16 lists these names for one edge-bff only.
findings.evidence: Code as cited. EXEC.md Phase 1 step 4 already says that changing EDGE_MFA_KEY after enrolment invalidates every authenticator. A second service, duplicated or configured by hand, holds its own copies, and a later rotation on one service splits them.
findings.failure_scenario: Different EDGE_MFA_KEY: the admin's authenticator enrolled on live fails on beta, the failures count in the shared mfa_totp lock, and enrolling on beta replaces the nonce, so the live authenticator stops working. Different EDGE_SESSION_SECRET: every throttle (sign-in 10 per 15 min, codes 20 per day, emails 10 per day) is counted twice over, once per site, and a cookie moved between sites reads but cannot write. Different EDGE_CODE_SECRET: a code mailed by one site fails on the other, while the one-live-code rule lets a request on one site consume the other site's code.
findings.general_class: Keyed hashes stored in a shared table where the key is per-service configuration. The Phase 5 webhook secrets and any later HMAC'd column follow the same rule.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c adds no keyed column in edge_bff.
findings.affects_beta_live: This finding exists only with two edge-bff services on one database.
findings.fix: In the beta/live design, make the live service's EDGE_SESSION_SECRET, EDGE_CODE_SECRET and EDGE_MFA_KEY Railway references to edge-bff's values, so one rotation reaches both. Record it in CONTRACT 16 and in railway.ts, and add a check in scripts/railway_reference_consumers.py that both services resolve to the same source.

checked: Branch r2-skew created at ae9a1d8f; Postgres cluster r2_skew (port 55531) used for every run and stopped at the end; nothing pushed, deployed, or sent to Railway or a remote database.

Read r1_seen.json (46 findings and the refuter notes), EXEC-MU-ACCOUNTS to the end, the Production environment decision (2bb4342f: beta at the Railway address, live at the user's domain, one environment), CONTRACT sections 0-3, 8b (3a, 3b, 3c in detail, 3b follow-up, deploy orders), 15 and 16, and RAILWAY_CHANGELOG entries for Phases 0-3b (deploy ids, rollback points, the order of uploads and pushes).

edge-bff and the database schema per phase: /ready probes (store.py:54-86), the lifespan latch, the old builds reading the new schema (Phase 0 build 637b0b96 sessions), the migrations 20261116_002 to 20261117_004 against the previous builds (no reader breaks; 20261117_002 drops users_email_key, which no earlier build reads), and the p3c-int migrations 20261118_001/_002/_100 against the deployed 3b edge-bff (with the switch off, the deleted backtest/screener families are not read because the owner is '*'). terminal-api 3c's /ready covers edge_owner_key.

edge-bff with the workers: allow/limits strictness in both workers (unknown key fails closed, an unknown id in allow is tolerated, absent allow means everything until step 3), the pre-3b workers refusing context.allow (848a9d41), and step 3 on p3c-int requiring allow. The backtest loop re-reads the principal at dispatch, and the AI worker re-checks before dispatch.

Throttle: HMAC key namespace per EDGE_SESSION_SECRET and its split under two secrets. The R1-8/R1-10 fixes (a changed key_hash label) would also reset or split live counters during a deploy overlap; this is only a note for the fix round, not reported.
Session resolution switch-off against switch-on in both directions: a switch-off row (user_id NULL) is refused with the switch on, which is safe; a switch-on row is accepted with the switch off (F1).

findings.title: L1: the hourly purge deletes a never-verified registration but every email_outbox row naming its address stays for ever; edge-bff cannot delete outbox rows at all
findings.root_cause: purge_pending (accounts.py:248-252, called from Store.cleanup_sessions store.py:354-358) deletes the users row, and identities and codes go with it (ON DELETE CASCADE). edge_bff.email_outbox names the person by value: it holds to_email and has no user_id (20261116_003:161-178), so neither the cascade nor the purge reaches it. edge_bff_runtime holds SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on the outbox, with no DELETE (20261116_003:224-225; the $verify$ block expects exactly that; scripts/provision_edge_bff_login.py:41 EXACT_GRANTS refuses any extra grant). No code deletes outbox rows (grep: no DELETE on email_outbox anywhere). CONTRACT sections 1 and 5 define no outbox retention. Only section 4 says 'A pending user is deleted 24 h after creation if never verified'.
findings.evidence: tests/test_r2_life.py::test_l1_the_purge_of_a_never_verified_registration_leaves_no_row_naming_its_address, at c9b5e53c on my cluster r2_life. A registration of someone.else@example.com is sent through a mock Resend (status sent, payload null), then its rows are aged by 25 h. Store.cleanup_sessions then runs as a login holding only edge_bff_runtime's grants. The users row is gone, but the outbox still holds [('register', 'sent')] for the address (to_email, purpose, created_at, sent_at, provider_id, idempotency_key 'code:<id>'). The test fails the same way on a git-archive extract of p3c-int 41067e7d.
findings.failure_scenario: With the switch on, anyone can type a stranger's address into /register (the 202 is the same for everyone). After 24 h the pending row with the names, phone and password verifier is deleted as CONTRACT promises. edge_bff.email_outbox still keeps that the address was registered, and when, for ever. The same holds for every code, account_exists and password_changed email of every account. In log mode (the dev default) it also keeps the rendered email. A retention policy or a deletion request cannot be honoured without a migration. The Privacy text (out of scope, the user's content) cannot state a retention for this data.
findings.general_class: Rows that name a person by value (an address) rather than by user_id escape both the cascade of a user deletion and every purge keyed on users. Instances: email_outbox.to_email (never removed); email_codes (cascaded on deletion, but the consumed codes of active accounts accumulate, and email_change keeps target_email, 20261116_003:118); email_suppression.email (kept on purpose); auth_throttle key hashes (purged after 2 days, fine). Where the purge runs: only inside the AI job worker's loop (worker.py:45-49), which starts only when /ready passed at start (main.py:272). Under C2-SKEW F3, a start during a database blip runs no purge at all until the next restart. The class reaches later phases: Phase 4's 'resend a code' and email change, and Phase 5 orders and events keyed by email. R1-42's proposed fix option 'have the purge skip accounts the audit names' would keep a never-verified registration's names, phone and verifier for ever once Phase 4 acted on it, so the fix should keep audit ids without an FK instead.
findings.affects_3c_why: 3c writes no outbox, code or account row. Its terminal owner rows are made only for signed-in principals, and a pending registration never has a session.
findings.affects_beta_live: Both websites would run the purge (idempotent, no worse). If the background loops get one owner per loop (EXEC Production environment, consequence 2), the outbox retention must belong to the same owner. A log-mode beta claims the rows of both sites and keeps their rendered emails in the payload beside the address (see L3).
findings.fix: Add a forward migration granting DELETE on edge_bff.email_outbox to edge_bff_runtime (update the $verify$ pattern and EXACT_GRANTS in scripts/provision_edge_bff_login.py). In Store.cleanup_sessions, delete the outbox rows of an address that has no non-pending account once its registration is purged. Also delete terminal rows (sent, failed, expired, suppressed) older than a retention the user decides. Keep at least the 60 s that FlowStore._may_send reads (auth_flows.py:142-143). Record the retention in CONTRACT sections 1 and 5 and in the README account section.
